Important new evidence

Two-year nicotine patch trial finds no cognitive benefit in MCI

In 348 adults with mild cognitive impairment, 24 months of transdermal nicotine did not improve the prespecified verbal-memory outcome versus placebo and caused more dizziness and treatment withdrawals; the newly posted registry results do not support clinical use.

Important new evidence•ClinicalTrials.gov results record•September 17, 2026

Two-year nicotine patch trial finds no cognitive benefit in MCI

In 348 adults with mild cognitive impairment, 24 months of transdermal nicotine did not improve the prespecified verbal-memory outcome versus placebo and caused more dizziness and treatment withdrawals; the newly posted registry results do not support clinical use.

Key quantitative results: For the primary International Shopping List Test immediate-recall outcome at month 24, least-squares means were 16.95 with nicotine and 16.59 with placebo; adjusted mean difference 0.37 points (95% CI −0.78 to 1.52; p=0.530). A complier analysis was also null (difference 0.12, 95% CI −1.27 to 1.51; p=0.868).

Registry ResultsManagementMild cognitive impairment

Added September 18, 2026 · NCT02720445; ClinicalTrials.gov results first posted 2026-09-17

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The official registry now supplies exact 24-month effect estimates for a long-running trial of an inexpensive, readily available intervention. Neither the primary memory outcome nor global, functional or cognitive secondary measures showed a convincing benefit, and attrition and adverse effects limit enthusiasm for off-label use.

Study design

Forty-one-site phase 2 trial that randomized 348 nonsmoking adults with mild cognitive impairment to transdermal nicotine (titrated from 3.5 mg to 21 mg daily) or placebo for 24 months, with quadruple masking and a three-week taper.

Key quantitative results

  • For the primary International Shopping List Test immediate-recall outcome at month 24, least-squares means were 16.95 with nicotine and 16.59 with placebo; adjusted mean difference 0.37 points (95% CI −0.78 to 1.52; p=0.530). A complier analysis was also null (difference 0.12, 95% CI −1.27 to 1.51; p=0.868).
  • Secondary estimates were similarly inconclusive: delayed recall difference 0.16 (95% CI −0.45 to 0.74), CDR-SB −0.09 (−0.50 to 0.32), ADCS-ADL −0.05 (−1.79 to 1.68) and post-hoc MMSE 0.61 (−0.14 to 1.35).
  • Completion was 91/171 with nicotine and 106/177 with placebo. Adverse-event withdrawal occurred in 28 versus 17 participants; dizziness occurred in 29/171 versus 8/176, headache in 13/171 versus 4/176, insomnia in 13/171 versus 5/176 and abnormal dreams in 12/171 versus 2/176. Serious adverse events occurred in 27/171 versus 24/176, with one death in each arm.

What changed

Detailed results were first posted to ClinicalTrials.gov on September 17, 2026, supplying exact 24-month efficacy, attrition and safety data beyond earlier topline reporting.

Strength of evidence

Randomized, masked, multicenter evidence with 24 months of treatment, but the result is currently registry-based and attrition was substantial, with only 91 nicotine and 106 placebo participants completing follow-up.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

The posted evidence does not support transdermal nicotine as a treatment for mild cognitive impairment and identifies a meaningful tolerability and discontinuation burden.

Field medical relevance

Useful for counseling about an accessible off-label intervention, for closing the loop on prior pilot signals and for informing whether additional nicotine studies should proceed without a stronger target-population or dosing rationale.

Access or reimbursement relevance

Transdermal nicotine is commercially available, but this study establishes no MCI indication, guideline endorsement, coverage policy or reason for unsupervised use.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Is this a newly published clinical-trial paper?
No. The qualifying development is the official results posting in ClinicalTrials.gov, so it is categorized as Registry Results rather than Clinical Trials.
Should patients with MCI try nicotine patches?
These results do not support that use. Nicotine also caused more dizziness and treatment withdrawals, and it has no established MCI treatment indication.
Was an Alzheimer biomarker used to select participants?
The registry result is not a central biomarker report and is not tagged Biomarkers.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Results are currently reported in the registry rather than a peer-reviewed primary manuscript
  • Substantial attrition over 24 months, with differential adverse-event withdrawals
  • The MCI population was not defined by a central Alzheimer biomarker question
  • Multiple secondary and post-hoc outcomes do not overcome the null prespecified primary result

Primary source · Structured registry record

Vanderbilt University Medical Center. Memory Improvement Through Nicotine Dosing (MIND) Study. ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02720445. Results first posted September 17, 2026.
